prompt: `curl -s http://localhost:3000/ | grep -c '<h2>'` prints `0`, and the same question to `/ssr` finds eight. Why?

choices.text: curl runs no script, and only `/ssr` has the products in its HTML
choices.why: Right. The home page's list is built by `app.js` in a browser; `/ssr` arrives with it written in.

choices.text: The home page was still loading when curl read it, so the list was cut short
choices.why: curl waits for the whole response; the products are simply not in it, however long you wait.

choices.text: `/` writes its product headings as `<h1>`, which this grep does not count
choices.why: Its cards use `<h2>` too, once a browser has drawn them; the HTML has no cards at all.

choices.text: curl is refused by the home page
choices.why: The server answers curl like any client; the answer just holds an empty list.

prompt: On a slow phone, what does a person see first on the server-rendered page that they do not see on the client-rendered one?

choices.text: A spinner while the products are fetched
choices.why: No product request is needed on `/ssr`: the products are in the document.

choices.text: Working buttons, before the HTML
choices.why: Nothing comes before the HTML, and the buttons work only after `/slow/ssr.js` has run.

choices.text: The products, as soon as the HTML arrives
choices.why: Right. They are written into the document, so they show without waiting for any script.

choices.text: Nothing different; the two pages are identical on screen at every moment
choices.why: They end up alike, but `/` shows an empty list until its script has run and asked.

prompt: When the browser builds the content from data a script fetched, the page uses ___ -side rendering.
The first test clicks Banana's button on `/ssr` and the click raises no error, yet the basket stays at 0. Why did Playwright click without complaint?

choices.text: The button was visible, stable and enabled, which is all its checks look at
choices.why: Right. Nothing on the outside of a button says whether it has a click handler.

choices.text: It clicks without checking anything
choices.why: It checks actionability before every click; the button simply passed.

choices.text: The button was covered by the toast
choices.why: `/ssr` has no toast, and a covered button would have made Playwright wait.

choices.text: The click was sent to the wrong card
choices.why: Any card would have done; no button had a handler yet.

prompt: In `app/routes/ssr.js`, for how many milliseconds does the server hold back `/slow/ssr.js`?
Suppose the server's pause were cut to 20 ms. What would the test that clicks at once most likely become?

choices.text: A test that always passes, because 20 ms is shorter than any click
choices.why: It would still click with no wait for the handler; a busy machine could still lose the race.

choices.text: A test that still always fails, because the click comes before any script
choices.why: With the gap that short, the script would often run before the click.

choices.text: A flaky test, passing or failing with the machine's speed
choices.why: Right. The race is still there, only narrower, which is the shape of lesson 14's flaky tests.

choices.text: A test that errors before it reaches the click
choices.why: Nothing before the click depends on the pause.

prompt: Why does `await expect(button).toBeEnabled()` before the click not fix the test on `/ssr`?

choices.text: It waits too long and the test times out
choices.why: It does not wait at all: the button is enabled from the start.

choices.text: The button is enabled from the start
choices.why: Right. A wait helps only if what it watches changes when the page becomes ready.

choices.text: Playwright has no such assertion for buttons
choices.why: It has it; it just watches the wrong property for this page.

choices.text: It only works on `<input>` elements, not buttons
choices.why: It works on buttons too.

prompt: Which of these wait for something that happens only after `ssr.js` has run? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `expect(page.locator('body')).toHaveAttribute('data-ready', 'true')`
choices.why: Right. The script sets the attribute as its last line.

choices.text: `page.waitForResponse('**/slow/ssr.js')`
choices.why: It fires when status and headers arrive, before the script has run.

choices.text: `expect(page.getByTestId('basket-count')).toHaveText('1')` after a click
choices.why: Right. Only a wired button can change the count, so this can only pass after the script ran.

choices.text: `expect(button).toBeEnabled()`
choices.why: The buttons are enabled in the server's HTML, before any script.

prompt: The developers agree to send the buttons `disabled` and enable each one in `ssr.js`. What happens to the first test, the one that clicks at once?

choices.text: It passes unchanged: the click now waits for the button to be enabled
choices.why: Right. Actionability already includes enabled, so the page's honesty does the waiting.

choices.text: It fails sooner, because Playwright treats a click on a disabled button as an error
choices.why: Playwright waits for a disabled button to become enabled before it gives up.

choices.text: It still fails, and now needs the marker as well
choices.why: The run in the section passed with no change to the test.

choices.text: It passes only with `--workers 1`
choices.why: Workers decide how many tests run at once, not how a click waits.

prompt: With `test.use({ javaScriptEnabled: false })`, how many products does `/ssr` show, and how many does `/` show?

choices.text: Eight and eight
choices.why: `/` needs `app.js` to draw anything, and it never runs.

choices.text: Eight and none
choices.why: Right. The server wrote `/ssr`'s products into the HTML; `/` waits for a script that never runs.

choices.text: None and none
choices.why: Switching scripts off does not remove what is already in the HTML.

choices.text: None and eight
choices.why: That is the two pages swapped.

prompt: The test `/ssr lists its eight products without a script` passes. A colleague wants to rename it `the shop works without JavaScript`. What is wrong with that?

choices.text: Nothing; both names describe the same check on the same page with JavaScript off
choices.why: One claims content, the other claims behaviour, and only content was checked.

choices.text: Test names may not contain the word JavaScript
choices.why: Playwright accepts any string as a name; the problem is what it claims.

choices.text: The new name would make the test fail, because Playwright matches it against the page
choices.why: A name changes nothing in what runs; it changes what a reader believes.

choices.text: The buttons do nothing without a script, and the test never presses one
choices.why: Right. A test proves what it asserts; this one asserts that products are listed.

prompt: Why does the second test, `/ lists nothing without a script`, carry a comment saying it is a fact and not a requirement?

choices.text: Playwright skips tests that have no comment
choices.why: Comments are ignored by the runner; they are for people.

choices.text: So nobody mistakes it for a requirement
choices.why: Right. The day the team wants products without JavaScript, this test is the one to turn round.

choices.text: Because the test fails and the comment explains why
choices.why: It passes; the comment explains what its passing means.

choices.text: To turn the check off when it runs on build servers
choices.why: A comment turns nothing off.

prompt: A test that asks only for the `request` fixture checks `/ssr`. What does it never do?

choices.text: Send an HTTP request
choices.why: Sending requests is all it does.

choices.text: Use the config's `baseURL` to turn `/ssr` into a full address
choices.why: It does: `request.get('/ssr')` resolves against it.

choices.text: Open a page, so no script on it ever runs
choices.why: Right. It reads the HTML as text, which is why it is fast and why it cannot see `/`'s products.

choices.text: Read the response body
choices.why: `.text()` reads it; that is how the test finds the headings.

prompt: A team checks `/ssr` only with HTTP tests that read its HTML. Which defect from this lesson would get past them?

choices.text: A product missing from the HTML that the server sends for `/ssr`
choices.why: That is exactly what the HTML test compares against the API.

choices.text: The second and a half when the buttons ignore clicks
choices.why: Right. The HTML was right throughout; the defect is in what happens after it arrives.

choices.text: A price written in the wrong format inside one of the cards
choices.why: The price is in the HTML, so a test that reads it can check it.

choices.text: The route answering `404`
choices.why: Any HTTP test sees the status first.

prompt: Match each question to the cheapest test in this lesson that can answer it.

pairs.left: Does the HTML of `/ssr` name every product?
Does a click on `/ssr` add to the basket?
pairs.right: A browser test that waits for the marker

pairs.left: Does `/ssr` show its products when scripts are off?

prompt: Put what happens on `/ssr` in order, from the request to a click that works.
items: The HTML arrives with the eight products in it
trap: The script is asked for only after `load`, so `goto` returns before it has even been requested.

prompt: Another shop renders on the server and sets no ready marker. Its buttons are enabled from the start. What should a tester do first?

choices.text: Add a fixed two-second wait before every click
choices.why: It slows every test and still fails the day the script takes longer.

choices.text: Retry each click until the basket changes
choices.why: A retried click can count twice once the handler arrives between tries.

choices.text: Wait for `networkidle` before each click and move on
choices.why: Its documentation discourages it for tests, and a page that polls never goes quiet.

choices.text: Ask for the buttons to start disabled
choices.why: Right. It fixes the page for people too, and Playwright's own check then does the waiting.

prompt: `npx playwright test tests/ssr.spec.js --repeat-each 5` with two workers once failed with `Received: "2"`. What is the likeliest cause?

choices.text: Two copies ran at once and shared the shop's one basket
choices.why: Right. One copy's click landed in the other's count; lesson 15 is about that.

choices.text: The marker was set before the buttons were wired
choices.why: `ssr.js` sets it on its last line, after the loop.

choices.text: The reset in `beforeEach` failed
choices.why: A failed reset would leave old items, not add one more during the test.

choices.text: Playwright clicked twice
choices.why: `click()` clicks once; the second item came from another copy of the test.
